"The Berlin team replied," Mohit said, not looking up from his laptop. "They want a second interview."
"Oh. That's great." Sudha folded a kurta very carefully. "When?"
"Next Thursday."
"Great."
"You keep saying great."
"It is great. For you."
"For us, I hoped."
Sudha put the kurta down. "Mohit, my parents are getting older. Papa's knee. I told you I wanted to stay in Jaipur."
"I know. I just thought, maybe for two years..."
"Let's talk about it after the interview. No point before."
"Yeah. After."
He went back to the laptop. She went back to folding. Neither of them said what both were thinking: that "after" had been the answer for four months now.

I'm Reena, and I think I knew by last spring that Joseph and I were walking in different directions. I'd started volunteering at weekends with a school project in the Nilgiris, and every time I came back to Kochi I felt more awake. I wanted to go there full-time. Live simply. Teach.
Joseph's dream was the opposite: a flat near his parents in Kakkanad, a steady bank job, Sunday mass with his family. Good dreams. Just not mine.
We did talk about it, in a way. "Maybe someday," he'd say. "Let's see how things are next year," I'd say. Our talks about the future got shorter and more polite, like two people being careful in a shop.
Looking back, the silence wasn't peaceful. It was both of us afraid to ask the question that might have an answer we didn't want.

qa.q: Where had Reena been volunteering at weekends?
qa.a: Reena had been volunteering at weekends with a school project in the Nilgiris.

qa.q: What were Reena and Joseph afraid of as their talks got short and polite?
qa.a: Both were afraid to ask the big question in case the answer was one they didn't want.

qa.q: What could they do instead of 'maybe someday'?
qa.a: They could sit down and say plainly what each wants, the Nilgiris or Kakkanad, and ask whether a shared path exists, perhaps with help from someone they trust.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Reena's weekends in the Nilgiris?
qa.a: Joseph may see them as a hobby and hope Reena will settle in Kochi, not realising how strongly they are pulling Reena away.

Lalit,

I'm writing this because every time we try to talk about it, we end up talking about dinner instead.

The Singapore offer is real. They want an answer by the 15th. I want to go. I've wanted something like this since college.

I know you want to stay in Jaipur, near your parents. I know your father's health is on your mind, and that you love our small life here: the Sunday market, your cricket, our balcony.

When I brought it up last week, you said, "Let's discuss it later." When I tried again on Friday, you said, "Sure, sure," and changed the subject. And I let you. I've been doing it too.

We've become polite about the biggest question we've ever had. I don't want polite. I want us to actually talk, even if it's hard.

Can we sit down on Sunday?

Vidya

qa.a: By the 15th.

qa.q: How does Vidya feel about their recent talks about the future?
qa.a: Vidya feels frustrated and worried that they have become polite and avoidant about the biggest question they've faced.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage?
qa.a: Sitting down on Sunday and talking honestly about Singapore and Jaipur, instead of leaving the big question for later.

qa.a: Lalit may feel anxious and torn, wanting stability near family and afraid of where the conversation leads.

You asked when things started to shift with Indu. I'm Gautam, and I think it was the evening she came home talking about the organic farm in Uttarakhand.

She'd visited it for a work story. She wanted to leave her newspaper job and move there, grow things, live simply. Her eyes were shining.

I'm an accountant in Lucknow. My parents are here. My whole life is here. I love our flat, my Sunday badminton, the chaat stall at the corner.

I said, "Sounds amazing." And then I asked if we should order dinner.

After that, every time she mentioned the farm, I said something polite. "Let's see." "Maybe someday." She stopped bringing it up so often. We still talked about groceries and films and my mother's birthday.

It felt peaceful. It wasn't. We were just being very careful not to ask the question neither of us wanted answered.

qa.a: In Uttarakhand.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel, looking back, about saying "Sounds amazing" and changing the subject?
qa.a: He feels regretful and uneasy, seeing now that his politeness was a way of avoiding a question he was afraid to answer.

qa.q: What could Gautam have done differently when Indu first talked about the farm?
qa.a: He could have asked her more about what she wanted and shared his own wish to stay, starting an honest conversation instead of a polite one.

qa.q: What might it be like for Indu when Gautam keeps saying "Maybe someday"?
qa.a: She may feel unheard and a little lonely, so she stops bringing up something that clearly matters to her.

January. Pema came back from a conference in Bengaluru buzzing about a start-up that wanted him. "They'd take me in March," he said. Urmila, who taught at the school down the lane from her parents in Gangtok, smiled and said, "That's great." Then she asked about the flight.

March, two months later. The start-up offer came in writing. Pema left it on the table. Urmila saw it and moved it to make room for the tea tray. Neither mentioned it at dinner. They talked about her mother's knee and the neighbour's new car.

May. Pema's friend asked, "So are you moving?" Pema said, "We haven't decided." In the taxi home, Urmila looked out of the window. Pema looked at his phone.

"We should talk about it," she said at last.

"Later," he said. "After your exams are marked."

She nodded. It was always later now.

qa.a: At the school down the lane from her parents in Gangtok.

qa.q: What does Urmila moving the offer letter to make room for the tea tray suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels uneasy and wants to avoid the question, afraid of what the answer might mean for their life near her family.

qa.q: What could Pema and Urmila do instead of saying "later"?
qa.a: Set a real time soon to talk openly about the offer and about staying near family, before the chance or the relationship slips away.

qa.q: How might Pema feel when Urmila smiles and asks about the flight?
qa.a: He may feel a little deflated, sensing she doesn't share his excitement but not knowing how to raise it.

grounding: Over months Pema is pulled toward a start-up job while Urmila wants stability near family, and their talks about the future become polite and postponed.

passage: You asked why I never took the Singapore job, Maria. Sit, your tea will go cold. At twenty-five, I, Rukmini, the eager young engineer, had an offer there. Anand, whom I was seeing then, had just bought a scooter to take his parents to the temple every Friday in Kochi. He wanted our life right there, near his mother's garden. I wanted the airport. We both knew it. Yet our talks became very polite. "How was work?" "Fine. Yours?" When the offer letter came, I left it in my drawer and said, "Let's discuss after Onam." After Onam, he said, "After my sister's exam." We kept pushing the big question to later, like a box nobody wanted to open. That box does not get lighter with waiting, Maria. It only gets heavier.
